metaData.originalTitle: How to Build an AI Support Agent That Knows When NOT to Answer Tickets
metaData.title: How to Build an AI Support Agent That Knows When NOT to Answer Tickets
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article presents an escalation-first architecture for building AI support agents that reliably know when not to answer tickets, using a pure-function decider and a two-judge consensus verifier.
metaData.summary: This article, written by a full-stack engineer who placed 9th out of 1,349 participants in a hackathon, argues that standard RAG-based AI support agents fail on sensitive tickets like fraud reports. The author proposes an 'escalation-first' design where a pure Python function, not an LLM, makes the routing decision. This decider routes tickets to one of three paths: a grounded reply, a polite template decline for benign off-topic requests, or an escalation to a human. The system also includes a two-judge consensus verifier with an arbiter for disagreements to ensure answer faithfulness. The article details the implementation, cost-saving measures like Jaccard pre-checks and caching, and honestly discusses five gaps in the author's own submission, emphasizing the critical importance of investing in a robust labeled dataset over over-engineering the pipeline.

mainPoints.point: The core design principle is to move the escalation decision out of the LLM and into a deterministic pure function.
mainPoints.explanation: Using an LLM to decide whether to answer a ticket is vulnerable to prompt injection, non-determinism, and rationalization drift. A pure Python function with auditable branches and unit tests is safer and more reliable.

mainPoints.point: The system uses three terminal paths instead of two: grounded reply, polite template decline, and human escalation.
mainPoints.explanation: A simple 'reply or escalate' model fails to handle benign off-topic requests. The third path allows the agent to absorb low-value queries with a template, reserving human attention for sensitive or risky tickets.

mainPoints.point: A two-judge consensus verifier with an arbiter provides a second safety net for answer faithfulness.
mainPoints.explanation: A single LLM verifier is fragile. Using two independent judges with different prompt framings and a third arbiter for disagreements creates a robust system for catching unfaithful or hallucinated responses.

mainPoints.point: The most critical lesson from the hackathon was to invest in a large, hand-labeled dataset before tuning the pipeline.
mainPoints.explanation: The author's main failure was tuning thresholds and rules against only 10 labeled rows. A larger, more representative labeled set is essential for reliable performance and prevents over-engineering on a flawed foundation.

keyQuotes: The design problem is not 'build a chatbot.' It's 'build something that knows the difference between the two and route accordingly'.
The fix is structural separation. Move the decision out of the language model entirely.
The rule is conservative by construction. The agent declines a ticket on its own only when both signals agree it is harmless.
The competitive edge for service businesses adopting AI isn't the automation. It's the escalation logic.
Don't measure your AI agent by how much it automates. Measure it by how reliably it knows what NOT to answer.
